clue.text: Finding fag end in fancy cat food is a catastrophe

indicators.note: in tells us the fag end goes inside the rearranged cat food
fancy as a verb or adjective suggests something elaborated or reworked, so the words cat food are rearranged

parts.note: the fodder, taken as written

indicators.note: the end of the word fag is its final letter, so only that is taken

parts.note: last letter of fag

explanation.surface: Someone finds a cigarette butt in a fancy tin of cat food and calls it a disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fancy' rearranges CAT FOOD to ACTOFOD, and 'in' puts G, the end of 'fag' (British slang for a cigarette), inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: An act of God is a natural disaster no one can be blamed for, such as a flood or earthquake.

clue.text: Bill's regular companion in lovemaking?

parts.note: the phrase 'bill and ...' means to kiss and murmur endearments, like courting doves; the word paired with bill is the dove's soft call

explanation.walkthrough: Bill looks like a man's name with a partner, but it is the verb in the idiom 'bill and coo', where lovers behave like billing doves.
explanation.definitionFit: In the idiom about lovers kissing and murmuring, the dove's soft murmuring sound always follows bill.

clue.text: Present state supporting old refuge

indicators.note: in a down clue the supporting piece sits beneath, so the present-state phrase comes after the old abbreviation

parts.note: 'as is' means in its present state, unchanged

explanation.surface: A tale of a present-day nation propping up an old place of asylum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present state' reads as a modern country, but it is the phrase AS IS, as goods are sold unaltered.
explanation.definitionFit: An oasis is a fertile spot in the desert, and figuratively any place of shelter or relief.

clue.text: Slag off deserving author

indicators.note: off suggests something gone wrong or not right, so the letters of slag are rearranged

parts.note: the fodder, taken as written
deserving and worthy both mean meriting something

explanation.surface: Insulting an author who deserves better.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slag off' is British slang for criticise harshly, but here 'off' rearranges SLAG to GALS.
explanation.definitionFit: John Galsworthy was the English novelist who wrote The Forsyte Saga and won the Nobel Prize in Literature.

clue.text: One sketching plans omits first rule — that's not so sensible

indicators.note: omits means leaves something out, here the letter from rule

parts.note: a drafter draws up plans and technical drawings

indicators.note: first picks the opening letter of the word rule

parts.note: first letter of rule

explanation.surface: A draughtsman who ignores the first rule of the job is being foolish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'omits' takes R, the first letter of 'rule', out of DRAFTER.
explanation.definitionFit: Daft means silly, so the comparative describes someone or something less sensible.

clue.text: Cheers and jeers are forbidden

definitions.note: the answer is a plural noun, things that are forbidden, so the definition works together with 'are'

parts.note: ta and cheers are both British informal ways of saying thank you
boos and jeers are both noises of disapproval

explanation.surface: A crowd is told that both applause and catcalls are banned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheers' is not applause but the British thank-you, TA.
explanation.definitionFit: Taboos are subjects or acts that custom or religion prohibits.

clue.text: Star pilot regularly forms part of this group

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter of star pilot is taken

parts.note: the letters picked from, taken as written

explanation.surface: A top pilot is a member of some team or squad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters of STAR PILOT.
explanation.definitionFit: A trio is a set of three, and the letters picked make up a group of that size.

clue.text: Change fibre seal — it protrudes slightly

indicators.note: change as an instruction to alter, so the letters of fibre seal are rearranged

parts.note: the fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: A maintenance note: replace the fibre seal because it is sticking out a little.
explanation.definitionFit: Bas-relief is sculpture in which the figures project only a little from the flat background.

clue.text: Bad team standard is hard to explain

definitions.note: the answer is a noun; the definition is a playful description of something notoriously hard to explain

parts.note: food that has gone off has gone bad
a side is a team in sport
a rule is a standard or norm

explanation.surface: A poor team's standard of play defies explanation.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a jokey description rather than a synonym: football's offside law is famous for confusing spectators.
explanation.definitionFit: Football's offside law is the classic example of a sporting regulation that newcomers find baffling to understand.

clue.text: Diplomat shows downside with those leading such unhealthy lives

parts.note: the pros and cons: a con is a disadvantage

indicators.note: those leading means the front letters of each of the following words

parts.note: first letter of such
first letter of unhealthy
first letter of lives

explanation.surface: An envoy reveals the drawbacks of living with people of unhealthy habits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'downside' points to the pros and cons, where a con is a disadvantage.
explanation.definitionFit: A consul is an official appointed by a government to protect its citizens' interests in a foreign city.

clue.text: Protective mechanism ensures triumph against dangerous opponents

parts.note: against signals the opposite: the opposite of triumph is to fail
opponents signals the opposite: the opposite of dangerous is safe

explanation.surface: A security system guarantees victory over a perilous enemy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'against' and 'opponents' ask for opposites: the reverse of triumph, then the reverse of dangerous; 'ensures' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A fail-safe is a backup system designed to prevent harm when a machine or process breaks down.

clue.text: Plant two drugs

parts.note: 'two drugs' asks for two slang drug names; the first is horse, slang for heroin
the second drug is weed, slang for cannabis

explanation.walkthrough: The clue says 'two drugs': one word for heroin and one for cannabis, side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: Horseweed is a weedy North American plant of the daisy family, also called Canadian fleabane.

clue.text: Glad to be recovered from exposure?

parts.note: to be over an illness is to have recovered from it
the moon is a bared backside, as in mooning someone

explanation.surface: Someone is delighted to have got over a bout of hypothermia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exposure' suggests hypothermia, but it is mooning, showing one's bare bottom; being over that gives the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Being over the moon is a British idiom for being extremely pleased or delighted.

clue.text: Weak parliament holds president back

indicators.note: back means the whole result is read in reverse order
holds means contains, so the parliament word wraps around the president letter

parts.note: a diet is a legislative assembly, as in Japan's Diet

explanation.surface: A feeble assembly is restraining its head of state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holds' puts P inside DIET to give DIPET, and 'back' turns that round.
explanation.definitionFit: Tepid means lukewarm, and figuratively half-hearted or lacking enthusiasm or force.

clue.text: Variable level holds key when reversing fundamental theory

indicators.note: reversing means the combined level-and-key letters are read backwards
holds means contains, so the level word wraps around the key word

parts.note: a tier is a level or layer
key and vital both mean crucial
in algebra x, y and z stand for variables, so Y is used here

explanation.surface: A physics textbook: the variable level contains a key once the theory is turned around.
explanation.walkthrough: The level holding the key gives TIVITALER, which turns round to RELATIVIT; Y, the algebraic variable, goes last although the clue names it first.
explanation.definitionFit: Einstein's theory of relativity underpins modern physics' understanding of space, time and gravity.

clue.text: Send out from Dover, for instance

parts.note: ex is Latin for from, as in ex-works
Dover is an English Channel port, so it is an example of the word

explanation.surface: Shipping goods abroad from Dover.
explanation.walkthrough: DOVER is the English Channel port facing France, so it is defined by example.
explanation.definitionFit: To export is to sell and ship goods to another country.

clue.text: Charge when flower pruned in private borders

indicators.note: in places the pruned flower between the edges of private
the borders of a word are its first and last letters

parts.note: outer letters of private
a rose is a flower
pruned means cut back

explanation.surface: A gardener is accused over a rose cut back in someone's private flower beds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pruned' is not deletion here: it is CUT, a synonym, set after the flower.
explanation.definitionFit: To prosecute is to bring legal proceedings against someone, formally charging them with a crime.

clue.text: Broadcast second number on old record next

indicators.note: broadcast means spoken over the air, so the answer is what the record side sounds like

parts.note: the B-side of a vinyl single carried its second song

explanation.surface: A DJ plays the flip side of an old single on air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' suggests radio play, but it signals a sound-alike: B-SIDE, the second track on a vinyl single.
explanation.definitionFit: Beside means at the side of, adjacent to or alongside something.

clue.text: Award for pub in old city

indicators.note: in puts the pub letters inside the old city

parts.note: Troy was the ancient city of the Trojan War
PH, public house, is the map abbreviation for a pub

explanation.surface: A prize given to a bar in a historic town.
explanation.walkthrough: PH (public house) is the abbreviation British maps use for a pub.
explanation.definitionFit: A trophy is a cup or other prize presented to the winner of a contest.

clue.text: Chap's complaint when hearing what the Wright brothers achieved

indicators.note: when hearing signals that the words are as heard, so a phrase sounding like them is entered

parts.note: the Wright brothers made the first powered flight, so with them man flew

explanation.surface: A man moans about his ailment while hearing about the pioneers of aviation.
explanation.walkthrough: The Wright brothers' achievement was that MAN FLEW, which said aloud is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Man flu is the jokey name for a mild cold supposedly exaggerated by the male sufferer.

clue.text: Right to become affectionate when there's no time?

indicators.note: read from the answer's side: the answer with no time letter becomes the cuddling word, so that letter goes back inside it

parts.note: to spoon is to cuddle or kiss affectionately

explanation.surface: A lover's question about getting cosy when there is no time to spare.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue works backwards: the answer, once it has no T, becomes SPOON. So build it forwards by putting T for time inside SPOON.
explanation.definitionFit: Spot on is a British informal phrase for exactly correct or accurate.

clue.text: Handle first fruit picker held in both hands

indicators.note: held in means gripped inside, so the fruit picker sits between the two hands

parts.note: left and right hands, L and R
in Genesis Eve picked the forbidden fruit

explanation.surface: An apple picker's tool is gripped in both hands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'both hands' are L and R, left and right; EVE, who plucked the forbidden fruit, sits between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A lever is a bar or handle used to operate a machine.

clue.text: Rich spent wildly to acquire muscle

indicators.note: wildly means in a chaotic, uncontrolled way, so the letters of rich spent are rearranged

parts.note: the fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: A wealthy person splashes out to build up their physique.
explanation.definitionFit: A sphincter is a ring-shaped muscle that closes an opening in the body.

clue.text: Drink available when college finished each year

parts.note: up means over, as in 'time's up'
PA, per annum, means each year

explanation.surface: Tea is served once the college term ends every year.
explanation.walkthrough: PA is per annum, Latin for each year; a cuppa is British slang for a cup of tea.
explanation.definitionFit: A cuppa is an informal British word for a cup of tea, the everyday hot beverage.

clue.text: Gear placed around loch that covers a lot of Scotland

definitions.text: that covers a lot of Scotland
definitions.note: the answer is a noun; this describes it as a garment covering many Scotsmen

indicators.note: placed around means the gear word wraps around the loch letter

parts.note: kit is gear or equipment
L is an abbreviation for loch, a Scottish lake

explanation.surface: Gear laid out around a lake covering much of the Scottish landscape.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is playful: not the land of Scotland but its people, many of whom wear the garment.
explanation.definitionFit: The kilt is the knee-length tartan skirt traditionally worn by Scottish men, so it covers many Scots.

clue.text: Explode elite agenda trying to appeal to everybody

parts.note: pop means burst, as a balloon explodes
U is shorthand for upper class, the social elite
an agenda is a list of items to discuss

explanation.surface: A politician vowing to blow up the elite's plans to win over the masses.
explanation.walkthrough: U stands for upper class, a British label from the 1950s 'U and non-U' debate on posh usage.
explanation.definitionFit: A populist politician pitches policies at ordinary people's concerns, seeking broad mass support.

clue.text: Better finish off performance that's not been prepared

indicators.note: finish off means the final letter is cut away from the word for better

parts.note: to better something is to improve it

explanation.surface: Advice to polish off a performance that was under-rehearsed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finish off' drops the last letter, E, of IMPROVE.
explanation.definitionFit: Improv is short for improvisation, theatre or comedy made up on the spot without a script.

clue.text: Have an obligation to participate in rising casework

indicators.note: in a down clue rising means the letters are read from bottom to top, backwards
participate in means to take part, so only part of the word casework is used

parts.note: the letters searched, taken as written

explanation.surface: A duty to join in a growing caseload.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to participate in' finds EWO in casEWOrk, and 'rising' turns it upwards in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: To owe is to be under a duty to pay or repay something, a debt or a favour.

clue.text: Trendy outlet for make up

parts.note: in means fashionable, as in 'the in thing'
a vent is an opening that lets air or gas out

explanation.surface: A fashionable shop selling cosmetics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'make up' looks like cosmetics, but it is the verb meaning to fabricate.
explanation.definitionFit: To invent a story is to fabricate it, creating it from imagination.

clue.text: One criticising terribly easy yarn

indicators.note: terribly suggests something done badly or chaotically, so the letters of easy yarn are rearranged

parts.note: the fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: A critic slates a dreadfully simple story.
explanation.definitionFit: A naysayer is a person who habitually objects, denies or speaks negatively about proposals.
